newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Mar 26.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Mar 26.

text.p: Onlookers clapped and cheered last night as rescuers freed a man trapped for eight hours in mud and water six metres down a Wellington stormwater drain. Page 1.

A proposed driver's licence the size of a credit card that would have a photograph and bar code could be used as an instant identification card, Transport Minister Jenny Shipley said on Tuesday. She said the two most likely uses for the card would be for buying cigarettes and alcohol. The proposal was part of tougher rules for drivers recommended in a report by the Land Transport Safety Authority. Page 1.

National MP John Banks told Parliament's privileges committee on Tuesday that he feared a drunken Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters would hit him during a late-night altercation in a corridor at Parliament. "If Mr Peters had struck me and knocked me down I would have had to defend myself ... I knew the man was drunk and I didn't want to fight this man," Banks said.
Peters said he had had a small amount to drink "like about 75 percent of MPs" but it had had no bearing on his behaviour. Page 1.

Ministers wrangling over trout fishing rights are due to meet after Easter to try to resolve the issue that is splitting the cabinet and the coalition government. A senior government source said the ministers were to meet on Tuesday but the talks were postponed till after Easter following media reports on the row over whether the government should back an appeal against the Wanganui District Court ruling that Maoris may fish for trout without a licence in some circumstances. Page 2.

Labour Minister Max Bradford expects to announce soon how a review of Employment Court decisions will be carried out. Bradford said the Labour Department was planning the review, and it was possible an independent body would be used to carry it out. The review of Employment Court and Court of Appeal decisions in personal grievance and procedural matters was signalled in the Coalition agreement. Page 2.

Foreign Affairs Minister Don McKinnon on Tuesday rejected ACT NZ leader Richard Prebble's suggestion that the National government last year forced Radio New Zealand to agree to move from Broadcasting House to make way for the new ministerial building. Both McKinnon, who was leader of the House when the building's design was chosen, and State-Owned Enterprises Minister Jenny Shipley dodged Prebble's questions on whether the previous government offered RNZ $3 million in compensation for the move or whether Radio NZ was seeking an extra $4.5 million for its new studios. Page 2.

Renegade backbencher John Banks accused Prime Minister Jim Bolger on Tuesday of cheating New Zealanders, saying he had done it before and he feared Bolger would do it again. The attack on Bolger, which does not bode well for the long-term future of the Coalition Government's one-seat majority, came in front of Parliament's privileges committee and before a large gathering of journalists. Page 2.

Labour leader Helen Clark has called on women MPs to join a campaign against compulsory superannuation. "There can be no doubt that New Zealand superannuation paid to all New Zealanders over 65 in their retirement offers the most certainty to women," she said. "Compulsory superannuation schemes may work for those on good incomes with 40 years' continuous work, but the lifetime working patterns of most women do not fit that model." Page 2.

A Maori group trying to claim crown forestry land has spent about $2 million on research and legal costs, according to the Crown Forestry Rental Trust, four times the average cost for preparing a claim. The sum is the biggest single bill for putting together a Maori claim on crown land, but what group was given the money remains a secret. In the past seven years, up to the end of this month, the trust has paid out about $27.5 million in helping 56 Maori groups make land claims. Page 14.

The Crown Forestry Rental Trust may be close to resolving a dispute with the Land Information department involving millions of dollars in Crown forestry licence fees. Crown Forestry Rental Trust collects about $33 million in licence fees from forestry companies using Crown land. The interest on that money is used by the trust to help Maori groups prepare land claims on the forestry land. Page 14.

Airways Corporation has headed off a possible prosecution for anti-competitive behaviour by submitting a timetable to the Commerce Commission for the introduction of non-subsidised prices for contestable air traffic control services. Commission chairman Alan Bollard said the corporation was making progress to change its pricing system and the commission did not intend taking enforecement action against it. But if progress was not satisfactory the commission would have the option of enforcement action. Page 14.

Kapiti-Horowhenua power supply company Electra has pledged a freeze on prices till May 1999. The freeze comes on top of recent rebates and discounts, but also after a rise in off-peak charges for about five percent of Electra's 35,000 customers. Chief executive Rob Steele said on Tuesday that the freeze would apply unless exceptional circumstances applied. Electra had hedging contracts through the buying group PowerBuy, and a long-term contract with Trans Power. Page 14.

AMI Insurance will ask its 260,000 members to approve a combination of trust and limited liability company structure at an extraordinary meeting in Christchurch in Christchurch on April 30 to comply with the Companies Act 1993. Under the act all companies must re-register by June 30. There was no provision under the act for a mutual structure such as AMI's which is owned by members rather than shareholders. Page 14.

The sale of Works Civil Construction and Works Consultancy netted the Crown $39.37 million profit, according to the December half-yearly report of Works and Development Services COrporation. The sale of Works Geothermal resulted in a loss of $244,000. The subsidiary companies were sold for $89.52 million net of sale costs, realising a surplus above book value of $39.12 million. Page 14.

Shipping interests firmly oppose any form of privatisation of the Port of Napier. Port users met as Hawke's Bay Regional Council prepares to make decisions on capital restructuring of the port company and privatisation. At the Chamber of Commerce-sponsored meeting, the port users unanimously opposed any form of privatisation. They said the port's profits should go toward cutting costs and promoting the Hawke's Bay economy. Page 15.

NZ Post's year to March profit would be well down last year's record net $72.5 million but would be on budget, chief executive Elmar Toime said on Tuesday. "The level of profitability will be a good deal less than our previous yar -- that's right on target," Toime said. A key cause was the price reduction for letters from 45 cents to 40 cents last year. This would take NZ Post from a level of "exceptional high" profitability to a "very good" level, he said. Page 15.

Southland's The Power Company has announced a net profit of $2.36 million for the six months to December 31, 1996 compared with a net profit of $792,000 for the corresponding period in 1995. Directors said the profit represented a 7.2 percent return on shareholders funds and was close to the rate targeted in the statement of intent. Page 15.
